evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The Duffy antigen/chemokine receptor, DARC, is a gene that encodes a surface glycoprotein.
source: For example, the Duffy antigen/chemokine receptor, DARC (also known as ACKR1), is a gene that encodes a surface glycoprotein.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DARC.

claim: A single mutation producing the Duffy-null version of a surface glycoprotein does not bind to P. vivax, preventing parasite invasion of host cells and most disease.
source: It is a classic example of adaptation in human evolution, with a single mutation producing the Duffy-null version of a surface glycoprotein that does not bind to P. vivax, preventing parasite invasion of host cells and most disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Duffy-null allele.

claim: Studies from multiple African populations have repeatedly found strong signatures of selection in human genomes at the DARC locus, likely because of its function in preventing P. vivax malaria.
source: Studies from multiple African populations have repeatedly found strong signatures of selection in human genomes at the DARC locus, likely because of its function in preventing P. vivax malaria (McManus et al., 2017; Kwiatkowski, 2005; Hamid et al., 2021; Pierron et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DARC and its expression levels have been implicated in parasite invasion or disease in multiple other primates with P. vivax relatives, including South American and African monkeys.
source: This gene and its expression levels have also been implicated in parasite invasion or disease in multiple other primates with P. vivax relatives, including South American and African monkeys (Camargos Costa et al., 2015; Tung et al., 2009; McHenry et al., 2010; Gunalan et al., 2019; Trujillo and Bergey, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hemoglobin S (HbS) provides resistance to P. falciparum malaria through changes to red blood cell morphology, decreasing parasite invasion, and, in some cases, causing sickle cell disease and other hemoglobin disorders.
source: Another classic example of human adaptation involves resistance to P. falciparum malaria also through changes to red blood cell morphology, such as hemoglobin S (HbS), decreasing parasite invasion, and, in some cases, causing sickle cell disease and other hemoglobin disorders (Kwiatkowski, 2005; Ha et al., 2019; De Sanctis et al., 2017; Luzzatto, 2012; Kuesap et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Ebel et al., 2017 found widespread phylogenetic signatures of adaptation in hundreds of genes that interact with malaria parasites.
source: More generally, Ebel et al., 2017 found widespread phylogenetic signatures of adaptation in hundreds of genes that interact with malaria parasites.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Parasites have complementary proteins that bind receptors on the surface of host red blood cells in order to enter host cells, notably including Duffy-binding proteins (DBPs) and reticulocyte-binding proteins (RBPs).
source: Parasites have complementary proteins that bind receptors on the surface of host red blood cells in order to enter host cells. These notably include Duffy-binding proteins (DBPs) and reticulocyte-binding proteins (RBPs) (Adams and Mueller, 2017; Lim et al., 2017; Su et al., 2020; VanBuskirk et al., 2004; Carlton et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: In vitro studies of P. knowlesi show that a junction does not form between host cell proteins and parasite when DBP is deleted.
source: In vitro studies of P. knowlesi show that a junction does not form between host cell proteins and parasite when DBP is deleted (Singh et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: P. vivax has recently been found to infect red blood cells of Duffy-negative people in Ethiopia and Madagascar, suggesting that alternative pathways to invasion exist.
source: However, P. vivax has recently been found to infect red blood cells of Duffy-negative people in Ethiopia and Madagascar, suggesting that alternative pathways to invasion exist (Ménard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference from the observation.

claim: Within-species genetic diversity across 11 genes in the P. vivax RBP family is hypothesized to mediate parasite-binding affinity.
source: Similarly, within-species genetic diversity across 11 genes in the P. vivax RBP family is hypothesized to mediate parasite-binding affinity (Lim et al., 2016), perhaps suggesting a role for between-species variation in host interactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves speculation.

claim: The first whole genomes from P. simium support a role for DBPs and RBPs in parasite evolution to new hosts or host specificity.
source: The first whole genomes from P. simium support a role for DBPs and RBPs in parasite evolution to new hosts or host specificity (Mourier et al., 2021; de Oliveira et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Population-genetic studies identified variants in RBPs that differed between human infections and those found in great apes; however, no significant difference in binding affinity was identified for parasites to great ape versus human red blood cells.
source: For example, population-genetic studies identified variants in RBPs that differed between human infections and those found in great apes; however, no significant difference in binding affinity was identified for parasites to great ape versus human red blood cells, suggesting that these RBP differences are not functionally critical for host specificity (Loy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference from experimental data.

claim: Multiple genes in red blood cell invasion pathways have been implicated in the host specificity of Laverania parasites, and host switching of P. falciparum based on comparative genomic approaches.
source: Multiple genes in red blood cell invasion pathways have also been implicated in the host specificity of Laverania parasites, and host switching of P. falciparum based on comparative genomic approaches (Martin et al., 2005; Rich et al., 2009; Rayner et al., 2011; Otto et al., 2018; Galaway et al., 2019; Plenderleith et al., 2019; Proto et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Galaway et al., 2019 found that the inferred ancestral protein of RH5 had similar binding affinity for gorillas and humans, perhaps aiding in early transfer of the population that became modern P. falciparum in humans.
source: Galaway et al., 2019 used ancestral sequence reconstruction for reticulocyte-binding-like homologous protein 5 (RH5) and quantified differences in binding affinity for human, gorilla, and chimpanzee cells. They found that the inferred ancestral protein had similar binding affinity for gorillas and humans, perhaps aiding in early transfer of the population that became modern P. falciparum in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves speculation about the implications.

claim: The modern P. falciparum version of RH5 is highly human-specific.
source: This is in contrast with the modern P. falciparum version of RH5, which is highly human-specific (Wanaguru et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in the protein-binding systems for red blood cell invasion have been implicated in P. knowlesi host switching.
source: Changes in the protein-binding systems for red blood cell invasion have also been implicated in P. knowlesi host switching (Moon et al., 2016; Dankwa et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Immune response genes such as AMA1, MSP1, CSP, and the var and pir gene family variants bind to host receptors, are involved in immune evasion and have been associated with disease severity.
source: These incredibly diverse genes, such as AMA1, MSP1, CSP, and the var and pir gene family variants, bind to host receptors, are involved in immune evasion and have been associated with disease severity (Tetteh et al., 2009; Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019; Conway, 2015; Neafsey et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: var genes such as PfEMP1 have been proposed as vaccine targets.
source: Understanding the strain-specific immune responses and range of natural genetic variation is particularly important because var genes such as PfEMP1 have been proposed as vaccine targets, and expression of var genes has been shown to change in response to treatments (Bachmann et al., 2019; Jensen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Vaccines developed against P. falciparum have had mixed success based on the genetic diversity of parasites.
source: Similarly, vaccines developed against P. falciparum have had mixed success based on the genetic diversity of parasites (Thera et al., 2011; Neafsey et al., 2015; Ouattara et al., 2015; Graves et al., 2016; Laurens et al., 2017; Bailey et al., 2020; Bell et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The high levels of genetic variation in P. vivax have been proposed as a barrier to an effective vaccine.
source: Indeed, the high levels of genetic variation in P. vivax have been proposed as a barrier to an effective vaccine (Lim et al., 2017), and DBPs and RH5 have been proposed as vaccine targets for P. vivax and P. falciparum, respectively (Bustamante et al., 2013; Douglas et al., 2011; Camargos Costa et al., 2015; Chitnis and Sharma, 2008; Mueller et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: DBPs and RH5 have been proposed as vaccine targets for P. vivax and P. falciparum, respectively.
source: Indeed, the high levels of genetic variation in P. vivax have been proposed as a barrier to an effective vaccine (Lim et al., 2017), and DBPs and RH5 have been proposed as vaccine targets for P. vivax and P. falciparum, respectively (Bustamante et al., 2013; Douglas et al., 2011; Camargos Costa et al., 2015; Chitnis and Sharma, 2008; Mueller et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2016; Su et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mathematical modeling suggests that group size plays an important role in disease transmission dynamics and infection rates.

claim: Recent studies have produced hundreds to thousands of Plasmodium genome sequences from around the world, particularly P. falciparum samples from Africa and Asia, and to a lesser extent P. vivax.
source: Recent studies have produced hundreds to thousands of Plasmodium genome sequences from around the world, particularly P. falciparum samples from Africa and Asia, and to a lesser extent P. vivax (Hupalo et al., 2016; Pearson et al., 2016; Amambua-Ngwa et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Newer work has developed identity-by-descent and linkage-based summaries of genetic variation in Plasmodium species more suited to study recent population history.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A major challenge remains: the expected neutral genetic diversity in malaria parasites is unclear, limiting population-genetic inference.
source: Despite these advances, a major challenge remains: the expected neutral genetic diversity in malaria parasites is unclear, limiting population-genetic inference.
evidence: This represents a current limitation in the field.

claim: Plasmodium parasites undergo a complex life cycle through host and vector stages, with multiple steps involving processes expected to dramatically influence genetic variation, such as bottlenecks with transmission, rapid asexual population growth in primate hosts, and sexual recombination in vectors.
source: Plasmodium parasites undergo a complex life cycle through host and vector stages. Multiple steps involve processes expected to dramatically influence genetic variation, such as bottlenecks with transmission, rapid asexual population growth in primate hosts, and sexual recombination in vectors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Plasmodium life cycle and its genetic consequences.

claim: The combination of life cycle stages makes genetic variation difficult to predict or fit to common models, such as Wright–Fisher.
source: The combination of these stages makes genetic variation difficult to predict or fit to common models, such as Wright–Fisher (Parobek et al., 2016; Chang and Hartl, 2015; Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A handful of studies have begun to address the challenge of understanding genetic variation by using simulation approaches, making substantial progress linking epidemiological and population-genetic models.
source: A handful of studies have begun to address the challenge of understanding genetic variation by using simulation approaches, making substantial progress linking epidemiological and population-genetic models (Chang and Hartl, 2015; Chang et al., 2013; Hendry et al., 2020; Watson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Figure 1 shows a bipartite plot to visualize malaria parasite sharing among primate hosts with host and parasite phylogenies at the genus and subgenus level, respectively.
source: Using the databases of the occurrence of Plasmodium species in primates presented here, Figure 1 shows a bipartite plot to visualize malaria parasite sharing among primate hosts with host and parasite phylogenies at the genus and subgenus level, respectively.
evidence: This describes what is shown in Figure 1.

claim: At the species level, Laverania species are primarily primate genus-specific.
source: At the species level, Laverania species are primarily primate genus-specific, with P. reichenowi, Plasmodium billcollinsi, Plasmodium billbrayi, and Plasmodium gaboni present in chimpanzees, and P. praefalciparum, Plasmodium blacklocki, and Plasmodium adleri present in gorillas.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1.

claim: P. malariae-related and P. vivax-related species often infect many NHP where they occur.
source: In contrast, P. malariae-related and P. vivax-related species often infect many NHP where they occur.
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and Figure 1.

claim: At the subgenus level, most parasites appear to be generalists, infecting diverse primate families, except for P. ovale relatives who are found only in great apes.
source: At the subgenus level, most parasites appear to be generalists, infecting diverse primate families, except for P. ovale relatives who are found only in great apes.

claim: Human P. falciparum infects fewer NHPs than P. vivax relatives.
source: Consistent with the pattern of specialist Laverania and generalist P. vivax relatives, human P. falciparum infects fewer NHPs than P. vivax relatives, and few Laverania species have been observed in humans today (but see Ngoubangoye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Few Laverania species have been observed in humans today.
source: Consistent with the pattern of specialist Laverania and generalist P. vivax relatives, human P. falciparum infects fewer NHPs than P. vivax relatives, and few Laverania species have been observed in humans today (but see Ngoubangoye et al., 2016).

source: In contrast, multiple P. vivax relatives have been found to naturally infect humans, including P. knowlesi, P. cynomolgi, and P. simium, yet only P. vivax itself is widespread (with potentially increasing infection of P. knowlesi).

claim: Only P. vivax itself is widespread among P. vivax relatives that infect humans.
source: In contrast, multiple P. vivax relatives have been found to naturally infect humans, including P. knowlesi, P. cynomolgi, and P. simium, yet only P. vivax itself is widespread (with potentially increasing infection of P. knowlesi).

claim: P. simium and P. vivax have only been found in a handful of South American monkey genera despite extensive sampling.
source: For example, while P. vivax relatives are generalists infecting all primate families considered here, substantial variation within lower taxonomic levels is observed; P. simium and P. vivax have only been found in a handful of South American monkey genera despite extensive sampling (Figure 2), and P. vivax is rarely observed in African monkeys, though its relative within the same subgenus relative Plasmodium gonderi infects them.

claim: P. vivax is rarely observed in African monkeys.
source: For example, while P. vivax relatives are generalists infecting all primate families considered here, substantial variation within lower taxonomic levels is observed; P. simium and P. vivax have only been found in a handful of South American monkey genera despite extensive sampling (Figure 2), and P. vivax is rarely observed in African monkeys, though its relative within the same subgenus relative Plasmodium gonderi infects them.
evidence: This is based on the data discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Plasmodium gonderi infects African monkeys.
source: For example, while P. vivax relatives are generalists infecting all primate families considered here, substantial variation within lower taxonomic levels is observed; P. simium and P. vivax have only been found in a handful of South American monkey genera despite extensive sampling (Figure 2), and P. vivax is rarely observed in African monkeys, though its relative within the same subgenus relative Plasmodium gonderi infects them.
evidence: This is based on the data discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Parasites from across the Plasmodium phylogeny regularly infect human populations.
source: Notably, parasites from across the Plasmodium phylogeny regularly infect human populations.
evidence: This is based on the data and knowledge discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The two most common human-infecting malaria parasites, P. falciparum and P. vivax, are from highly divergent parts of the Plasmodium phylogeny and are thought to represent independent zoonoses.
source: In particular, the two most common human-infecting malaria parasites, P. falciparum and P. vivax, are from highly divergent parts of the Plasmodium phylogeny and are thought to represent independent zoonoses.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic and evolutionary data discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The phylogeny of Plasmodium largely corresponds to geographic regions where the parasites are found – with P. vivax-related more common in Asia and South America, and P. falciparum and Laverania spp. in Africa.
source: Though host specificity appears correlated with phylogenetic relationships, the difference in host specificity may derive from ecological causes instead of or in addition to phylogenetics. The phylogeny of Plasmodium largely corresponds to geographic regions where the parasites are found – with P. vivax-related more common in Asia and South America, and P. falciparum and Laverania spp. in Africa – making the effects of phylogeny and geography difficult to disentangle.
evidence: This is based on the geographic distribution data discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The effects of phylogeny and geography are difficult to disentangle for Plasmodium.
source: Though host specificity appears correlated with phylogenetic relationships, the difference in host specificity may derive from ecological causes instead of or in addition to phylogenetics. The phylogeny of Plasmodium largely corresponds to geographic regions where the parasites are found – with P. vivax-related more common in Asia and South America, and P. falciparum and Laverania spp. in Africa – making the effects of phylogeny and geography difficult to disentangle.

claim: Faust and Dobson, 2015 identified species and regions that are likely undersampled with respect to parasite diversity, suggesting that new primate malaria parasites may occur in African monkeys and lemurs.
source: Faust and Dobson, 2015 identified species and regions that are likely undersampled with respect to parasite diversity, suggesting that new primate malaria parasites may occur in African monkeys and lemurs.

source: Updating their database here, we see that even areas that are predicted to be unlikely to introduce new parasite species, such as Southeast Asia and South America, still have substantial undersampling of known parasite diversity and range (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on the updated database and Figure 2 presented in the manuscript.

claim: Garamszegi, 2009 found an association between host and parasite phylogenies consistent with co-divergence at the family level, though the result was not statistically significant at the genus level.
source: For example, Garamszegi, 2009 tested whether malaria parasites of the same taxonomic group tend to infect primate hosts of similar taxonomic group or geographic region. Co-occurrence between host and parasite genera suggests a history of co-divergence and host specialization, whereas large differences may suggest recent host switching or host generalism. They found an association between host and parasite phylogenies consistent with co-divergence at the family level, though the result was not statistically significant at the genus level; parasites tended to infect closely related hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Major barriers exist to application and interpretation of quantitative methods for understanding parasite distributions, including uncertainty in parasite phylogenetic relationships, incomplete host sampling in the wild, and inconsistencies in parasite species naming.
source: However, major barriers exist to application and interpretation of these methods directly to the currently available data. These barriers include uncertainty in parasite phylogenetic relationships, incomplete host sampling in the wild, and perhaps most critically, inconsistencies in parasite species naming that are often confounded or defined by the host in which they are sampled.
evidence: This represents current limitations in the field.

source: Figure 2A and B show the distribution of P. knowlesi and P. cynomolgi cases, respectively, in both humans and NHPs. Reported cases of P. knowlesi in humans have occurred throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Lao, Myanmar, Indonesia, Cambodia, and Thailand, whereas primate infections have primarily been documented in Malaysia.

claim: Primate infections of P. knowlesi have primarily been documented in Malaysia.
source: Figure 2A and B show the distribution of P. knowlesi and P. cynomolgi cases, respectively, in both humans and NHPs. Reported cases of P. knowlesi in humans have occurred throughout Southeast Asia, including Malaysia, Lao, Myanmar, Indonesia, Cambodia, and Thailand, whereas primate infections have primarily been documented in Malaysia.

source: P. cynomolgi is present in primates throughout South Asia, though the range often does not overlap with known human infections (Figure 2C; Zhang et al., 2016; Imwong et al., 2019; Grignard et al., 2019; Hartmeyer et al., 2019; Raja et al., 2020).

claim: Variation in sampling effort drives the estimated species distributions of P. cynomolgi, especially outside Malaysia.

claim: P. inui is a strong candidate for future zoonotic transmission because it shares a host, some potential vectors, and environment with the known zoonotic parasites P. cynomolgi and P. knowlesi.
source: P. inui is a strong candidate for future zoonotic transmission because it shares a host, some potential vectors, and environment with the known zoonotic parasites P. cynomolgi and P. knowlesi (Baird, 2009; Coatney et al., 1966; Maeno et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on shared ecological factors, supported by citations.

claim: P. simium is known primarily from the Atlantic Forest region in Southeastern Brazil, infecting only a few American NHPs.
source: In South America, P. malariae and P. brasilianum are found throughout the continent and are able to infect a large number of primate species, whereas P. simium is known primarily from the Atlantic Forest region in Southeastern Brazil (though there have been recent reports in Colombia as well), infecting only a few American NHPs (Figures 1 and 2b; de Alvarenga et al., 2015, Brasil et al., 2017; Rondón et al., 2019).

claim: There have been recent reports of P. simium in Colombia.

claim: The presence of P. malariae/P. brasilianum throughout much of South America suggests a wider distribution of human infections is possible.
source: Currently, known outbreaks of primate Plasmodium in human populations are from a limited number of locations; however, the presence of P. malariae/P. brasilianum throughout much of South America suggests a wider distribution of human infections is possible, and may already be occurring unreported since these parasites produce less severe disease (Lalremruata et al., 2015; Brasil et al., 2017).

claim: Zoonotic malaria emergence may be more closely linked to the overlapping presence of NHP and vector populations than to human population density.
source: Comparing Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, we see multiple regions with zoonotic malaria transmission despite low human population densities. That is, zoonotic malaria emergence may be more closely linked to the overlapping presence of NHP and vector populations.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the figures.
